chunks.text: 2.1 3D Shape Reconstruction Methods 3D shape reconstruction methods employ deep learning to estimate complete body models from incomplete inputs. Wu, et al. Wu et al. (2016) introduced a 3D Generative Adversarial Network that learns a probabilistic latent space of 3D shapes using volumetric convolutions to synthesize and interpolate 3D shapes. Yuan, et al. Yuan et al. (2018) proposed Point Completion Network (PCN), an encoder-decoder model using a coarse-to-fine decoding strategy to infer complete dense point clouds. Chibane, et al. Chibane et al. (2020) developed Implicit Feature Network (IF-Net), which uses 3D convolutions to create multi-scale feature tensors and then classify deep features from these tensors to represent and reconstruct 3D surfaces. Yan, et al. Yan et al. (2022) introduced ShapeFormer, a transformer-based network encoding incomplete shapes into quantized tokens and estimating complete shapes using learned shape priors. Although effective in multimedia applications, these methods face two key challenges when applied to medical imaging: (i) the lack of publicly available large datasets pairing clinically truncated whole-body surfaces with complete reference surfaces, and (ii) the need to handle scans in which entire regions, such as the forearms or hands, may be completely absent. 2.2 Parametric Body Template Mesh Fitting Methods Parametric fitting methods estimate complete body models by aligning a body template mesh (fitting), typically SMPL Loper et al. (2015) , to incomplete inputs. Optimization-based methods achieve this by minimizing discrepancies in attributes, such as landmark distances and surface alignment, framing the process as an optimization problem. Bhatnagar, et al. Bhatnagar et al. (2020) proposed IP-Net, combining implicit function learning and semantic correspondences to refine SMPL fitting to sparse inputs. Liu, et al. Liu et al.

(2021) incorporated an occlusion-aware voting mechanism and used joint confidence to identify occluded joints and complete their features for SMPL mesh estimation. Feng, et al. Feng et al. (2023) introduced ArtEq, which directly predicts SMPL shape and pose using part detection and articulated SE(3)-equivariant networks to generalize across unseen poses. Jang, et al. Jang et al. (2023) fitted an SMPL mesh to sequential partial point clouds using a motion-aware variational autoencoder with kinematic priors to estimate a complete body model. Originally designed for multimedia applications, these methods are generally developed using non-clinical data, and their application to medical imaging must account for differences in patient positioning and scan coverage. Sequence-based methods additionally utilize temporal information that is unavailable in single, static medical images acquired in supine positions, thus limiting their direct applicability. 2.3 Image Compensation and SMPL-Based Body Model Fitting in Medical Applications Prior medical-imaging studies have addressed two related but distinct problems: compensation for limited-FoV image truncation and SMPL-based body model fitting to medical images or external body surfaces. Zamyatin et al. Zamyatin and Nakanishi (2007) developed a truncation correction approach for CT reconstruction FoV extension using sinogram information. Fonseca et al. Fonseca et al. (2021) evaluated a U-Net-based extended-FoV CT reconstruction method for radiotherapy-related applications. Arabi and Zaidi Arabi and Zaidi (2020) investigated a deep learning-based object completion approach using a dilated CNN with residual connections to compensate for body truncation in PET/MRI attenuation correction. These approaches reconstruct or compensate for missing image and attenuation-map information rather than estimate complete patient body models with continuous surface representations.

In contrast, MedBOE estimates a complete continuous patient body surface model for geometric and BHM analysis, which is complementary to image-domain truncation compensation. A second line of work has used SMPL-based fitting in medical imaging to infer body composition or internal anatomical structures from external body surfaces. Keller, et al. Keller et al. (2024) fitted SMPL to complete body models reconstructed from extended whole-body MRI images acquired using a specialized protocol for assessing adipose tissue distribution, enabling prediction of internal adipose compartments from complete patient body models. Shetty, et al. Shetty et al. (2023) estimated internal organ positions from external body surfaces by fitting the SMPL mesh to incomplete body models using a multi-stage optimization guided by manually annotated landmarks and surface distances. Although these studies demonstrate the utility of SMPL in medical imaging, their model construction relies on complete body coverage obtained using specialized imaging protocols or semi-manual external-surface fitting procedures that are difficult to scale. Furthermore, their primary aim was not the fully automated estimation of complete external patient body models from routine whole-body medical images with missing body regions. 3 Method MedBOE estimates complete patient body models from whole-body medical images through a three-module pipeline (Fig. 1 ). The body model reconstruction module (Fig. 1 (i)) generates incomplete patient body models from the whole-body images and automatically annotates the body-surface landmarks on the reconstructed models (Fig. 1 (b)). The global parametric fitting module (Fig. 1 (ii)) fits a SMPL template mesh to the incomplete patient body models and produces the fitted SMPL model (Fig. 1 (c)). The missing body region estimation and surface deformation module (Fig. 1 (iii)) estimates the missing body regions (red in Fig.

1 (d)) from the fitted SMPL mesh and stitches them to the incomplete patient body models to construct initial complete body models (Fig. 1 (d)). The fitted SMPL mesh is then further deformed to the initial complete body models, producing the final complete patient body models (Fig. 1 (e)). 3.1 SMPL Template Mesh The SMPL template mesh Loper et al. (2015) represents the human body as a triangulated mesh with 6,890 vertices, parameterized by body shape β \beta , pose θ \theta , and global translation t t . β \beta is modeled using low-dimensional principal component analysis coefficients derived from a statistical body shape space, while θ \theta is defined through a 24-joint kinematic skeleton. The mesh is deformed using Linear Blend Skinning, with joint regressor 𝒥 ⁡ ( β ) \mathcal{J}(\beta) , blend weights 𝒲 \mathcal{W} , and pose-dependent shape variations B ​ P ​ ( θ ) BP(\theta) . The final mesh M M is computed as: M = W ⁡ ( T ¯ + B ​ S ​ ( β ) + B ​ P ​ ( θ ) , θ , 𝒥 ⁡ ( β ) , 𝒲 ) , M=W\left(\bar{T}+BS(\beta)+BP(\theta),\theta,\mathcal{J}(\beta),\mathcal{W}\right), (1) where T ¯ \bar{T} is the canonical template mesh, 𝒲 \mathcal{W} is the blend weight, B ​ S ​ ( β ) BS(\beta) and B ​ P ​ ( θ ) BP(\theta) are the shape and pose blend shapes, respectively. Refer to Loper et al. Loper et al. (2015) for further details. 3.2 Body Model Reconstruction Module Whole-body images were segmented using a pre-trained nnU-Net Isensee et al. (2021) to isolate the patient’s body. The resulting binary masks were reconstructed into incomplete body models using the marching cubes algorithm Lorensen and Cline (1987) (Fig. 1 (b)). These models were smoothed using Taubin’s algorithm Taubin (1995) and simplified via Schroeder’s decimation Schroeder et al. (1992) . Patient metadata (gender, weight, height) was extracted from the image headers. Body landmarks were automatically annotated using the Deep Virtual Marker Kim et al.

(2021) , which assigned each vertex of the incomplete patient body model a 99-dimensional virtual-marker label vector. For each model, sparse landmarks (black dots in Fig. 1 (b)) were obtained by selecting the vertex with the highest response for each of the 99 virtual-marker labels. Dense landmarks were represented by the 99-dimensional virtual-marker label vector assigned to each vertex, visualized as surface colors in Fig. 1 (b). The same procedure was applied to the default male and female SMPL meshes. Only sparse landmarks with confidence greater than 0.5 were included in the sparse landmark distance term. 3.3 Global Parametric Fitting Module The global parametric fitting module aligns a gender-specific SMPL template mesh to the reconstructed incomplete patient body model (Fig. 1 (b)). The module uses six attributes: sparse landmark distance ( E Sparse E_{\mathrm{Sparse}} ), surface distance ( E Dist E_{\mathrm{Dist}} ), pose prior ( E Prior E_{\mathrm{Prior}} ), weight consistency ( E Weight E_{\mathrm{Weight}} ), self-intersection penalty ( E Contact E_{\mathrm{Contact}} ), and dense landmark distance ( E Dense E_{\mathrm{Dense}} ). These attributes collectively enforce global and local alignment, inspired by prior studies Shetty et al. (2023) ; Clever et al. (2023) . Specifically, E Sparse E_{\mathrm{Sparse}} and E Dense E_{\mathrm{Dense}} constrain anatomical correspondence from virtual-marker labels and improve landmark-level alignment. E Dist E_{\mathrm{Dist}} uses a modified symmetric Chamfer distance with correspondence filtering to improve global geometric alignment. E Prior E_{\mathrm{Prior}} constrains unrealistic joint configurations and stabilizes pose estimation using VPoser Pavlakos et al. (2019) and MaxMixturePrior Bogo et al. (2016) . E Weight E_{\mathrm{Weight}} constrains SMPL shape parameters using patient weight and improves patient-specific body size matching by leveraging BetaNet Clever et al. (2023) .

E Contact E_{\mathrm{Contact}} constrains mesh self-collisions and reduces anatomically implausible overlap, such as hand penetration into the body. The global parametric fitting module optimizes the weighted sum of these attributes ( E Fit E_{\mathrm{Fit}} ) by adjusting the fitting SMPL’s β \beta , θ \theta , and t t : E Fit = \displaystyle E_{\mathrm{Fit}}={} λ Sparse ​ E Sparse + λ Dist ​ E Dist + λ Prior ​ E Prior \displaystyle\lambda_{\mathrm{Sparse}}E_{\mathrm{Sparse}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{Dist}}E_{\mathrm{Dist}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{Prior}}E_{\mathrm{Prior}} (2) + λ Weight ​ E Weight + λ Contact ​ E Contact + λ Dense ​ E Dense , \displaystyle+\lambda_{\mathrm{Weight}}E_{\mathrm{Weight}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{Contact}}E_{\mathrm{Contact}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{Dense}}E_{\mathrm{Dense}}, The parameters β \beta , θ \theta , and t t were initialized to zero and jointly optimized using the Adam optimizer Kingma and Ba (2015) over 500 iterations, with each attribute scaled by λ x \lambda_{x} . 3.4 Missing Body Region Estimation and Surface Deformation Module The missing body region estimation and surface deformation module comprises coarse and fine stages. In the coarse stage, the fitted SMPL mesh (Fig. 1 (c)) is non-rigidly deformed to the incomplete patient body model (Fig. 1 (b)) to estimate missing body regions and construct an initial complete patient body model (Fig. 1 (d)). The coarse stage uses four attributes: sampled surface distance ( E Surf E_{\mathrm{Surf}} ), edge length ( E Edge E_{\mathrm{Edge}} ), Laplacian smoothness Desbrun et al. (1999) ( E Lap E_{\mathrm{Lap}} ), and normal consistency ( E Normal E_{\mathrm{Normal}} ). E Surf E_{\mathrm{Surf}} compares valid overlapping surface samples between the fitted SMPL mesh and the incomplete patient body model. The attribute minimizes squared surface distance while excluding non-overlapping regions using Euclidean-distance and surface angular-difference thresholds.

The torso and lower limbs were always included because they were consistently present in whole-body images. E Edge E_{\mathrm{Edge}} constrains changes in vertex edge lengths to preserve local mesh geometry during deformation. E Lap E_{\mathrm{Lap}} regularizes abrupt local vertex displacement and enforces local surface smoothness. E Normal E_{\mathrm{Normal}} minimizes orientation differences between neighboring surface elements and reduces orientation discontinuity. Together, these attributes coarsely deform the fitted SMPL mesh toward the incomplete patient body model while preserving local surface geometry and continuity. The coarse stage optimizes the weighted sum of these attributes ( E Coarse E_{\mathrm{Coarse}} ) over 100 iterations using the Adam optimizer Kingma and Ba (2015) : E Coarse = λ Surf ​ E Surf + λ Edge ​ E Edge + λ Lap ​ E Lap + λ Normal ​ E Normal , E_{\mathrm{Coarse}}=\lambda_{\mathrm{Surf}}E_{\mathrm{Surf}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{Edge}}E_{\mathrm{Edge}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{Lap}}E_{\mathrm{Lap}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{Normal}}E_{\mathrm{Normal}}, (3) After the coarse stage, the boundary of the incomplete patient body model was used to trim the deformed SMPL mesh, isolating estimated missing body regions (red in Fig. 1 (d)). These regions were stitched to the incomplete patient body model using Poisson surface reconstruction Kazhdan et al. (2006) , producing an initial complete patient body model (Fig. 1 (d)). In the fine stage, the fitted SMPL mesh is further deformed to the initial complete patient body model, formulating the problem as complete-to-complete alignment. This stage smooths visible discontinuities between estimated and existing regions and reduces residual discrepancies introduced during coarse estimation. The fine stage uses five attributes: Chamfer distance ( E CD E_{\mathrm{CD}} ), Chamfer normal ( E CN E_{\mathrm{CN}} ), volume consistency ( E Vol E_{\mathrm{Vol}} ), E Lap E_{\mathrm{Lap}} , and E Normal E_{\mathrm{Normal}} .

E CD E_{\mathrm{CD}} measures bidirectional nearest-neighbor point distances between the deforming SMPL mesh and the initial complete patient body model, reducing residual pointwise discrepancy. E CN E_{\mathrm{CN}} compares corresponding surface normals between the deforming SMPL mesh and the initial complete patient body model and improves local orientation consistency. E Vol E_{\mathrm{Vol}} constrains changes in the SMPL mesh volume to preserve patient-specific body size established during global parametric fitting. E Lap E_{\mathrm{Lap}} and E Normal E_{\mathrm{Normal}} were reused from the coarse stage. The fine stage optimizes the weighted sum of these attributes ( E Fine E_{\mathrm{Fine}} ) over 150 iterations using the Adam optimizer: E Fine = λ CD ​ E CD + λ CN ​ E CN + λ Vol ​ E Vol + λ Lap ​ E Lap + λ Normal ​ E Normal , E_{\mathrm{Fine}}=\lambda_{\mathrm{CD}}E_{\mathrm{CD}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{CN}}E_{\mathrm{CN}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{Vol}}E_{\mathrm{Vol}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{Lap}}E_{\mathrm{Lap}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{Normal}}E_{\mathrm{Normal}}, (4) Deformation was applied only to regions overlapping with the initial complete body model, determined by pointwise distance. To ensure anatomical completeness, the torso, legs, head, neck, and arms were forcibly included, while deformation of the forearms, hands, and feet was restricted to overlapping regions to avoid propagating discontinuities introduced in the previous step. By jointly optimizing these attributes, the module produces the estimated complete model with a smooth surface, geometric accuracy, and volumetric consistency (Fig. 1 (e)). Detailed formulations of attributes ( E x E_{x} ) used in the global parametric fitting and missing body region estimation and surface deformation modules are provided in Appendix 8 . 3.5 Implementation The body model reconstruction module was implemented using the VTK library Schroeder et al. (2000) and the official Deep Virtual Marker package Kim et al. (2021) .

The global parametric fitting and missing body region estimation and surface deformation modules were implemented in PyTorch with smplx and NVIDIA Kaolin Pavlakos et al. (2019) ; Paszke et al. (2019) ; Tsang et al. (2024) , incorporating official pretrained models of MaxMixturePrior, VPoser, E Contact E_{\mathrm{Contact}} , and BetaNet Clever et al. (2023) ; Pavlakos et al. (2019) ; Bogo et al. (2016) ; Müller et al. (2021) . Additional libraries, including SimpleITK, OpenCV, pyMeshLab, and pyMeshFix Lowekamp et al. (2013) ; Bradski and Kaehler (2008) ; Muntoni and Cignoni (2021) ; Attene (2010) , were employed for extracting and integrating missing body regions. The Adam optimizer was used with learning rates of 0.01 for global parametric fitting and the coarse stage of the missing region estimation and surface deformation, and 0.001 for the fine stage. In E Dist E_{\mathrm{Dist}} , correspondences were excluded when the Euclidean distance exceeded 0.1 m or 0.01 m, or when the surface-normal angular difference exceeded 45 ∘ 45^{\circ} or 30 ∘ 30^{\circ} , for SMPL-to-incomplete patient body model and incomplete patient body model-to-SMPL correspondences, respectively. In E Dense E_{\mathrm{Dense}} , correspondences were excluded when the Euclidean distance exceeded 0.1 m or when the surface-normal angular difference exceeded 45 ∘ 45^{\circ} . Pointwise distance thresholds for detecting overlapping regions were set to 0.01 m for the coarse stage and 0.005 m for the fine stage. Attribute weights ( λ x \lambda_{x} ) used in the global parametric fitting module are detailed in Table 1 . Early iterations prioritized E Sparse E_{\mathrm{Sparse}} and E Dense E_{\mathrm{Dense}} , followed by increased emphasis on geometric alignment ( E Dist E_{\mathrm{Dist}} ). The weight for E Weight E_{\mathrm{Weight}} was reduced to allow flexibility in adapting to the incomplete patient body model geometry.

E Prior E_{\mathrm{Prior}} remained constant, while E Contact E_{\mathrm{Contact}} was activated only during the final 100 iterations to reduce computation. These models were smoothed using Taubin’s algorithm Taubin (1995) and simplified via Schroeder’s decimation Schroeder et al. (1992) . Patient metadata (gender, weight, height) was extracted from the image headers. Body landmarks were automatically annotated using the Deep Virtual Marker Kim et al.

(2021) , which assigned each vertex of the incomplete patient body model a 99-dimensional virtual-marker label vector. For each model, sparse landmarks (black dots in Fig. 1 (b)) were obtained by selecting the vertex with the highest response for each of the 99 virtual-marker labels. Dense landmarks were represented by the 99-dimensional virtual-marker label vector assigned to each vertex, visualized as surface colors in Fig. 1 (b). The same procedure was applied to the default male and female SMPL meshes. Only sparse landmarks with confidence greater than 0.5 were included in the sparse landmark distance term. 4 Experimental Setting 4.1 Datasets 4.1.1 AutoPET Dataset AutoPET Gatidis et al. (2022) includes 1,014 PET-CT examinations of 900 patients acquired on a Siemens Biograph mCT PET-CT scanner. AutoPET was selected because it is a publicly available routine clinical PET-CT dataset in which transverse FoV limitations are directly relevant to complete external-body model estimation. After excluding cases lacking weight data ( n = 149 n=149 ), non-true whole-body scans ( n = 466 n=466 ), transverse FoV overflow of the body in PET ( n = 307 n=307 ), and one with motion artifacts, 91 images were retained (35 male, 56 female). The dataset was used in 5-fold cross-validation. Images lacking recorded body weight were excluded because E Weight E_{\mathrm{Weight}} uses patient weight. Ground truth (GT) body models were constructed by segmenting PET images (which have a wider transverse FoV than CT) and applying the marching cubes algorithm Lorensen and Cline (1987) . Incomplete body models were simulated by trimming GT models using a cylinder with a radius equal to 95% of the average CT transverse FoV radius, centered on the PET images, to replicate missing body regions typical in routine whole-body imaging. Representative front, left, and right views comparing the virtually trimmed model with the body model reconstructed from CT are provided in Appendix Fig. 6.

For arms-up and mixed (up & down) arm poses, parts of the forearms and hands were absent in the GT due to the diagnostic scan range. On average, the simulated trimming removed 1.75 ± \pm 1.62% (0.26–7.80%) of body volume and 4.46 ± \pm 3.84% (0.84–20.95%) of body surface area in males, and 1.32 ± \pm 1.33% (0.01–6.53%) of body volume and 3.74 ± \pm 3.10% (0.10–15.02%) of body surface area in females. 4.1.2 HIT Dataset The HIT dataset Keller et al. (2024) includes complete body segmentations from 419 MRI images (168 male, 251 female), acquired using a 1.5 T Siemens Magnetom Sonata MR scanner under a specialized protocol for whole-body adipose tissue mapping. Patients were scanned in a prone position (lying face down) with arms extended overhead and compressed within the scanner’s transverse FoV, which is smaller than that of most current CT and PET-CT scanners. The dataset includes GT SMPL meshes aligned to the segmentations and annotated with β \beta and θ \theta . A predefined split (train/val/test) was used: 136/17/15 for male and 201/25/25 for female subjects. GT body models were reconstructed from the segmentations using the marching cubes algorithm Lorensen and Cline (1987) . Incomplete body models were simulated using the same trimming method as in Section 4.1.1 due to the absence of original MRI FoV data. Additionally, regions extending 10 cm above the head were removed to reflect typical scan overage (Fig. 1 ). As patient weights were not provided, HIT weights were estimated by multiplying the GT model volumes by gender-specific mean body density Durnin and Womersley (1974) , following Choutas et al. Choutas et al. (2022) . This estimation approach was a pragmatic dataset-specific decision rather than the preferred input, because measured patient weight is preferable for the E Weight E_{\mathrm{Weight}} term. In AutoPET, a sufficient measured-weight cohort remained after exclusions, so cases without recorded weight were not assigned estimated weights.

This avoided mixing measured and estimated weights within the same validation cohort. In HIT, measured weights were not available; without weight estimation, HIT could not be used to evaluate regions such as hands and forearms, which were frequently absent in the AutoPET GT body models. On average, trimming removed 3.35 ± \pm 0.72% (2.09–4.83%) of body volume and 10.19 ± \pm 2.15% (7.06–15.29%) of body surface area in males, and 2.38 ± \pm 0.51% (1.59–3.42%) of body volume and 7.67 ± \pm 1.48% (5.88–11.86%) of body surface area in females. 4.2 Metrics 4.2.1 Accuracy of Estimated Complete Body Models MedBOE’s performance was evaluated by comparing estimated complete body models to corresponding GT models. To account for gender-related body shape variation, evaluations were performed separately for male and female models. For the AutoPET dataset, surface and volumetric comparisons were limited to regions present in the PET-derived GT models because parts of the forearms and hands were often excluded during acquisition (Section 4.1.1 ). Thus, AutoPET metrics evaluate accuracy over observable GT regions rather than complete accuracy over all body regions. In contrast, the HIT dataset allowed evaluation across the entire body. Additionally, estimated regions were assessed against the trimmed regions. Five metrics were used, following Jang et al. Jang et al. (2023) . Relative body surface area error (RBE) and relative volume error (RVE) quantified the mean absolute percentage errors in surface area and volume, respectively. Intersection over Union (IoU) quantified volumetric overlap between estimated and GT models. Chamfer distance (CD) represented the mean bidirectional closest-point distance between surfaces, and Hausdorff distance (HD) captured the maximum pointwise deviation. These metrics assessed differences in body size and volumetric overlap (RBE, RVE, IoU), as well as surface geometry (CD, HD).

4.2.2 Accuracy of BHMs Derived from Estimated Models Five BHMs (i.e., body surface area, body volume, and circumferences of the chest, waist, and hip) were derived from estimated complete body models and compared to those from GT models. These metrics were selected for their clinical relevance in applications, such as injected radiotracer activity regimens Xiao et al. (2021) and cardiometabolic risk assessment Janiszewski et al. (2007) , where accurate estimation of overall body size and key regional dimensions is critical. Body surface area was calculated from the total area of triangular facets, while body volume was computed by summing face-based volumetric contributions derived from vertex coordinates. Circumferences were derived using the method of Choutas et al. Choutas et al. (2022) , which computes the closed curves around predefined SMPL body landmarks (right mammary papilla, umbilicus, and pubic symphysis). Accuracy was expressed as mean percentage and absolute errors. Evaluation was limited to the HIT dataset, as GT circumference measurements were readily available only in this dataset. These measurements require body landmarks that can be automatically extracted, for example, from the GT SMPL meshes. GT values for complete body volume and surface area were also exclusive to HIT. 4.3 Runtime Delay Runtime delay was additionally measured to evaluate computational cost. Runtime delay was defined as the elapsed time required to estimate a complete patient body model from an input incomplete patient body model. Therefore, this measurement did not include image segmentation or incomplete patient body model reconstruction from the original medical images. Runtime was measured on a desktop computer with Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS, an Intel i7-8700K CPU, 64 GB memory and an NVIDIA TITAN V GPU. 4.4 Baselines MedBOE was compared with four state-of-the-art methods for complete body model estimation: IF-Net Chibane et al. (2020) , ShapeFormer Yan et al.

(2022) , ArtEq Feng et al. (2023) , and Point Completion Network (PCN) Yuan et al. (2018) , as introduced in Section 2 . These baselines were selected based on their relevance and availability of official implementations. IF-Net and ShapeFormer were trained and evaluated on the AutoPET and HIT datasets using incomplete body models automatically generated during training. PCN was trained on both datasets using paired GT and simulated incomplete body models; however, volumetric metrics were excluded for PCN because its point cloud output lacks surface representation. ArtEq was evaluated only on the HIT dataset due to its reliance on GT SMPL parameters. It was trained using SMPL meshes with GT parameters, with incomplete body models generated by randomly sampling the meshes. Because the official implementation settings failed to estimate complete models, the training epoch count was increased from 15 to 150. 4.5 Ablation Study We assessed the contribution of the missing body region estimation and surface deformation module by comparing the full pipeline with a variant that omits this module and directly outputs the fitted SMPL mesh after SMPL fitting. All other settings remained constant. 4.6 Statistical Analysis All results are reported as mean ± \pm standard deviation, with ranges indicated in parentheses (min–max). One-way ANOVA was used for multi-group comparisons, followed by post-hoc Tukey’s HSD tests. Paired comparisons were performed using the paired t-test. Male-female differences were assessed using Welch’s independent two-sample t-test Welch (1947) . The ANOVA-based comparisons were interpreted with consideration of their standard assumptions, including independent observations, approximately normally distributed residuals, and homogeneity of variance. Effect sizes are reported using Cohen’s d d , and uncertainty is reported using 95% confidence intervals (CIs), where applicable. Statistical significance was set to p < 0.05 p<0.05 .
